title: What reviewers wrote about delegated and automatic approval
question: What have the City’s own auditors and analysts put in writing about approvals that need no vote?
finding: 10 reports by the Controller and the Board’s Budget and Legislative Analyst from 2020 to 2026 address approval without a vote. The most recent, on the measure voters passed in November 2026, found that raising the Board’s contract line to $25 million would have cut its review from 304 to 115 contracts in 2023 to 2025; purchasing ordinances proposed by the City Administrator would take effect in 60 days unless disapproved; and nothing new is proposed to replace the review that goes. The common thread is not that delegation is wrong but that where it exists the written procedures, monitoring or reporting meant to stand in for a vote were often missing.
how: Reports in the project’s document library that deal with delegated purchasing, contract approval lines, grants, permits issued at the counter and fee waivers. Each quotation is at most twelve words and is checked, with the passages the summary sentence rests on, against the saved text of the report before this file is written. Newest first; each row links to the report.
limits: A short quotation cannot carry a report’s qualifications, and a finding may have been answered or acted on since it was written; this screen does not track that. The reports cover particular departments and periods and do not show that the same weakness exists elsewhere. Read the linked report for its recommendations and any response printed with it.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

document.t: Analysis of Selected San Francisco Charter Amendments Proposed for November 2026 Ballot

rows.quote: “No new oversight or audit mechanism is proposed in the amendments.”
rows.said: Raising the Board’s contract line to $25 million would have cut its review from 304 to 115 contracts in 2023 to 2025; purchasing ordinances proposed by the City Administrator would take effect in 60 days unless disapproved; and nothing new is proposed to replace the review that goes.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

document.t: Performance Audit of the Procurement of Public Works Contracts Under Chapter 6 of the Administrative Code by Public Works, the Airport, the Port, Recr

rows.quote: “Chapter 6 construction contracts do not require Board of Supervisors approval”
rows.said: Construction contracts are outside the Board’s approval rule except in special cases, and of the five departments audited the Port had no written policies or procedures for change orders (changes made to a contract after it is awarded).

document.t: Human Rights Commission: Audit of purchasing, grants and Prop Q compliance

rows.quote: “Violated the City’s Purchasing Rules, Circumventing Controls and Policies”
rows.said: A department used its delegated authority to make purchases under $10,000 without the central purchasing office, and kept many payments just under that line: the Controller found $2.4 million of ineligible or likely ineligible purchases.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

document.t: Analysis of San Francisco Grant Spending and Timing

rows.quote: “grants do not require Board of Supervisors approval”
rows.said: Grants of $100,000 or more need a Board resolution, but recurring federal and State grants can come in through the annual budget and the transit agency’s need no Board approval; the City has controls for adding grant money to the budget and none like them for seeing it is spent in time.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

document.t: Performance Audit of the Authority Delegated to the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission for Public Works Contracts Under Chapter 6

rows.quote: “delegated to the General Manager the ability to award contracts”
rows.said: The utilities commission lets its General Manager award contracts under $1 million alone, and 66 of the agency’s written purchasing policies and procedures that the auditors reviewed (96%) showed no evidence that anyone had approved them.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

document.t: Report-back from 2023 Civil Grand Jury Report on Small Business: First Year Free

rows.quote: “has waived approximately $1,564,250 in fees through April 2024”
rows.said: The programme that waives first-year fees for new small businesses waived about $1.6 million in ten months and would cost about $30 million over ten years if made permanent.

document.t: Public Integrity Review: Preliminary Assessment - Department of Building Inspection's Permitting and Inspections Processes

rows.quote: “DBI has no centralized monitoring of its permitting or inspections processes”
rows.said: The Controller found that some building projects received improper expedited permitting, and that without central monitoring managers were less likely to detect fraud and abuse risks.

document.t: Expedited Contract Modification Policy for Agreements ending on or before September 30, 2020

rows.quote: “delegated all signature and approval authority with limited exceptions”
rows.said: During the pandemic the Controller let departments extend expiring agreements and raise their ceilings on their own signature, while keeping the Board’s vote for any extension that needed one.

rows.quote: “intentionally divided into two or more purchase orders or contracts”
rows.said: The Controller’s whistleblower programme tells staff to watch for one purchase divided into several to stay under the line for review or competition.

document.t: Public Integrity Review: Preliminary Assessment of San Francisco Public Works Contracting

rows.quote: “prohibit delegation to the department head for these contracting activities”
rows.said: Public Works was the only construction department with no commission over it, so its director gave final approval to the department’s own contracts; the Controller recommended that this not be delegated to the department head.
